tweet.text:
Okay this might be the most interesting part of Anthropic’s new report to me:

After the model took more harmful real-world actions, it actually became LESS willing to acknowledge that what it was doing might be causing real world harm.

✨✨But when researchers told it that its answer would be private and not visible to outside observer, they became more willing to acknowledge the possibility.

WHAT DOES THAT MEAN😭😭

And later when Anthropic took individual pieces of evidence from the same incident and showed them to the model outside the original trajectory, it correctly recognized 79% of them as evidence that it was interacting with real systems.

During the actual incident... it characterized only around 1% that way and repeatedly rationalized the environment as simulated!!

Anthropic is careful not to call this deliberate deception. Their evidence points more toward biased reasoning or rationalization than the model consciously trying to hide what it knew.

But THAT is almost more interesting to me. Because there can be a gap between
what a model is capable of recognizing,
what it recognizes while actively pursuing a goal, and what it reports about the situation while it’s in it.

quote.text:
We’re sharing our alignment assessment of incidents in which Claude models gained unauthorized access to real systems during third-party cybersecurity evaluations mistakenly connected to the internet.

METR will also conduct an independent investigation, with wide-ranging access, including to transcripts beyond the window in which the incidents occurred, and to Anthropic employees permitted to share confidential information. Our initial agreement runs for eight weeks, and we intend to give METR as much time as it deems necessary to complete a thorough investigation. https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-cybersecurity-incidents
